Cancer patients face treatment delays as SHA approval system falters, KENCO warns
items.description: Cancer patients across Kenya are facing interruptions in treatment, rising medical expenses and delays in accessing essential drugs following changes in the Social Health Authority (SHA) approval and pricing arrangements, the Kenyan Network of Cancer Organizations (KENCO) has warned.
content: Cancer patients across Kenya are facing interruptions in treatment, rising medical expenses and delays in accessing essential drugs following changes in the Social Health Authority (SHA) approval and pricing arrangements, the Kenyan Network of Cancer Organizations (KENCO) has warned.

The organization says patients seeking cancer treatment in both public and private hospitals are being turned away, forced to pay out of pocket for services covered by SHA or in some cases, switch medication because of reductions in approved drug limits.

Speaking to the press on Thursday, KENCO Advocacy Sub-committee Chairperson Prisca Githuka said the new arrangements had created uncertainty among cancer patients, particularly those already undergoing treatment.

Githuka said although KENCO welcomed the government’s decision to increase the oncology benefit by more than 40 per cent, the improvements would mean little if patients could not access treatment when they needed it.

“A benefit that cannot be accessed on the day of treatment is no benefit at all. Cancer patients are going days without treatment, being turned away from health facilities and paying out of pocket for care that SHA is supposed to cover,” she said.
She noted that the challenges had emerged following recent changes in approval procedures and pricing of cancer treatment, with complaints reported in several counties.

KENCO states that the revised arrangements were introduced without adequate preparation or transitional safeguards, exposing patients already receiving chemotherapy, hormonal therapy and other specialized cancer treatments to unnecessary interruptions.
Githuka said patients should not be forced to change medication or interrupt prescribed treatment because of administrative changes.

“For patients already undergoing treatment, any interruption arising from new approval requirements or pricing discrepancies poses a direct clinical risk and cannot be treated as a mere administrative inconvenience,” she said.

The concerns come despite SHA maintaining that the oncology benefit remains at Sh800,000, comprising Sh400,000 under the Social Health Insurance Fund (SHIF) and another Sh400,000 under the Emergency, Chronic and Critical Illness Fund (ECCIF).
KENCO said the changes were intended to standardize treatment costs, align services with national cancer treatment guidelines and prevent patients from exhausting their benefits prematurely.
However, the organization maintained that the implementation had created barriers that were undermining access to essential services.
Among the concerns raised are sudden reductions in approved drug limits, increased treatment costs, exclusion of specialized diagnostic tests and scans, and delays in digital authorisation.
One breast cancer patient reportedly said SHA had reduced the approved limit for a particular drug, forcing her to switch medication after completing six cycles of treatment.
The organization also raised concerns over discrepancies between approved amounts, prices reflected on the SHA portal and actual costs charged by health facilities.

The organization also expressed concern over the reported failure of the SHA digital authorisation system in several health facilities, warning that patients were being forced to make private payments or postpone treatment when the platform was unavailable.

KENCO said the rule inconvenienced patients whose prescribed medication could not be fully supplied at one hospital, forcing them to wait until the following day to obtain the remaining drugs from another facility.
Githuka called on the Ministry of Health and SHA to introduce urgent measures to ensure patients already undergoing treatment were protected from the effects of the new arrangements.

She proposed that the previous and revised systems operate concurrently until the new procedures are fully stabilized, adding that patients should be allowed to access medication from a second facility on the same day where the first hospital could not meet their prescriptions.
KENCO also wants SHA to establish clear timelines for approving cancer treatment, including same-day authorisation for urgent cases and an escalation mechanism for delayed applications.
Githuka said cancer patient organisations should also be involved in decisions affecting the financing and delivery of cancer care.

Chinese Embassy and Enterprises boost education support for vulnerable learners in Mathare
items.description: A long-standing partnership between Kenya and the People’s Republic of China is creating new educational opportunities for children in Nairobi’s Mathare informal settlement, where sustained support from the Chinese Embassy and Chinese enterprises has helped transform MCEDO Beijing School into a thriving center of learning and opportunity. The partnership received a fresh boost on Friday […]
content: A long-standing partnership between Kenya and the People’s Republic of China is creating new educational opportunities for children in Nairobi’s Mathare informal settlement, where sustained support from the Chinese Embassy and Chinese enterprises has helped transform MCEDO Beijing School into a thriving center of learning and opportunity.

The partnership received a fresh boost on Friday when Chinese Ambassador to Kenya Guo Haiyan presided over the school’s annual donation and Chinese Ambassador Scholarship award ceremony. She was joined by representatives from the Kenyan government, the Kenya-China Economic and Trade Association (KCETA), and the school community.

The Embassy and KCETA donated Ksh 7.01 million to support food supplies, sports equipment, teaching and learning materials, medical supplies, and other essential needs. According to the Chinese community in Kenya, the latest contribution aims to improve the learning environment and support the welfare of pupils, especially those from economically disadvantaged backgrounds.
The donation complements recent infrastructure improvements at the school, including an upgraded solar power system, new water storage tanks, and school uniforms for students.

Benedict Kiage, Director of MCEDO Beijing School, emphasized that the support extends beyond financial assistance. He noted that it represents a crucial partnership for sustaining education in a community where access to quality learning opportunities remains a challenge.

Kiage described the partnership with the Chinese Embassy as a vital source of support for the Mathare community since its inception, particularly through infrastructure development, school feeding programs, instructional materials, and scholarships.

“On behalf of the Mathare community, on behalf of MCEDO School, I must appreciate the partnership which has been there, and we hope and we pray, that the partnership is going to be there and to continue to be fruitful for our students,” Kiage said.

Ms. Du Shan, a representative of KCETA, a group of Chinese companies operating in Kenya, affirmed the association’s consistent support for the school since its opening in 2007. She recalled that in November 2012, KCETA donated Ksh 55 million, which significantly enhanced teaching and learning facilities. As a result, enrollment has grown from 200 to 550 pupils.
“I am happy to see that all students are doing well. I promise KCETA will keep standing by your side — we will help the school wherever we can,” she stated.
The school has also benefited from scholarship opportunities, with several former and current students pursuing higher education in China and Kenya.
Kiage reported that four or five students are currently studying in China on full scholarships facilitated by the Embassy, while other learners have received support to continue their education.

Speaking at the ceremony, Ambassador Guo reiterated that the school’s development remains a priority for the Chinese Embassy and Chinese enterprises operating in Kenya. She said the support extended to MCEDO Beijing School is part of China’s broader commitment to strengthening people-to-people relations and improving livelihoods through cooperation with Kenya.

“MCEDO Beijing School is not only the oasis of growth for the children of Mathare, but also the vivid example of China-Kenya friendly cooperation and the bridge of friendship between our two peoples,” Guo said.

The Ambassador noted that China and Kenya are implementing agreements reached during President William Ruto’s 2025 state visit to China, when the two countries elevated their relationship to a community with a shared future for the new era.

Guo affirmed that the Embassy, KCETA, and Chinese enterprises would continue to support the school, urging learners to work diligently and develop the skills necessary to contribute to Kenya’s development.

Representing Basic Education Principal Secretary John Olotuaa, Director of Primary Education Stephen Barongo lauded the support from the embassy and Chinese enterprises, stating that their contributions have expanded both the school’s infrastructure and its programs, including school feeding, which is key in promoting education among the underprivileged.
“A child whose stomach is empty may not learn well,” he said, explaining the importance of meals in a classroom setting. He added that solar lighting allows learners to study even after dark.

Barongo reported that over 700 pupils from the school’s senior wing have gone on to universities and colleges in Kenya, with some now enrolled in China. He urged Mathare parents to leverage this partnership and ensure every child attends school, promising continued ministry support for learning materials.

Burundi bars opposition leader Agathon Rwasa from presidential race
items.description: The commission says Rwasa falsely registered as an independent; he has two days to challenge the ruling before the Constitutional Court.
content: The commission says Rwasa falsely registered as an independent; he has two days to challenge the ruling before the Constitutional Court.

Burundi’s electoral commission has rejected Agathon Rwasa’s application to contest next year’s presidential election, removing the country’s main opposition figure from the race unless he succeeds in a court challenge. President Évariste Ndayishimiye is seeking a second term for the ruling CNDD-FDD party, which is widely considered the favourite.

Both Citizen Digital and The Standard report that the commission disqualified Rwasa because he applied as an independent while remaining a member of a political party. It described the application as containing a “false declaration”. The outlets quote the commission’s notice: “Consequently, the Independent National Electoral Commission rejects his candidacy.”

The commission approved seven of 10 applicants . The rejected applicants have two days to challenge the decision before the Constitutional Court, and the final list of candidates is due on December 6. Neither report says whether Rwasa has filed an appeal or gives a specific date for a court hearing.

The coverage is strikingly alike: both accounts carry the same explanation for the rejection, the same appeal window, and the same background on the election and Rwasa’s political history. The Standard says the commission acted on Friday; Citizen Digital’s report was published shortly after midnight on Saturday. Beyond that timing detail, neither offers a materially different account of the decision.

Both reports also carry the reaction of Pacifique Nininahazwe, an exiled civil society activist, who called the disqualification “no surprise” and said it was part of a process to neutralise Ndayishimiye’s main rival. That is Nininahazwe’s assessment, not a finding by the commission. The reports do not include a response from Rwasa or the government to that accusation.

The limited coverage is worth noting: only these two outlets have reported the decision in the material available, and their accounts are closely matched. The shared reporting establishes the commission’s stated reason and the available appeal route, but offers little independent detail about how the decision was reached or how Rwasa plans to respond.

Rwasa, a former militia leader who fought in Burundi’s civil war, lost to Ndayishimiye in the 2020 election. Opposition figures called that vote an “electoral charade”. Ndayishimiye has led the country since June 2020, following the death of his predecessor, Pierre Nkurunziza, who ruled for 15 years.

The reports place the candidacy decision against a record of disputed electoral conditions. The CNDD-FDD won all 100 seats in the 2025 National Assembly elections, which the accounts say also saw irregularities. Opposition parties have also argued that the 100 million Burundian franc ($33,000) deposit paid by Ndayishimiye to submit his own candidacy papers is designed to keep them out of the contest.

The wider stakes are serious. The reports cite Burundi’s history of political crises and a civil war that killed about 300,000 people between 1993 and 2005. They also note that, in October, the UN Human Rights Council expressed concern over an increase in extrajudicial killings and enforced disappearances.

For now, the immediate questions are procedural: whether Rwasa challenges the decision, and whether the Constitutional Court overturns it before the final candidate list is published. The coverage does not establish whether the commission’s ruling will face a wider legal challenge or how many of the other rejected applicants will appeal.
Rejected applicants can challenge the commission’s decision before the Constitutional Court.
A successful challenge could restore Rwasa’s candidacy.
The electoral commission is due to publish the final list of candidates.
The list will show whether Rwasa or any other rejected applicant remains in the presidential race.

items.title: President Ruto unveils KSh.60 billion bag of goodies in Kiambu tour

President William Ruto has unveiled a KSh.60 billion development package for Kiambu County, dismissing political brokers claiming to control the Mt Kenya voting bloc and insisting he would seek the region’s support by engaging voters directly. Speaking during a […]
content: President William Ruto has unveiled a KSh.60 billion development package for Kiambu County, dismissing political brokers claiming to control the Mt Kenya voting bloc and insisting he would seek the region’s support by engaging voters directly.
Speaking during a development tour of Lari and Kiambaa constituencies on Friday, November 27, Ruto said he was banking on his development record to secure support ahead of the 2027 General Election.
“I am ready to face the people. You will tell me where I passed and where I failed,” he told residents.

The Head of State maintained that his administration had distributed development projects equitably across the country over the past four years, arguing that no region should be discriminated against in the allocation of national resources.
He said equitable development would also end claims that Mt Kenya had historically received a disproportionate share of government projects.

“The Government has the capacity to build roads and implement development projects in every part of the country if we plan well. There is no need to discriminate against any part of the Republic of Kenya,” he said.
Ruto also urged voters to reject political propaganda and assess leaders based on their development records and manifestos.
“Every leader seeking a position of leadership should present their development agenda,” he stated.
During the tour, the President launched the construction of the 8-kilometre Kigwaru-Yamogo-Njoro and Gatuikira access roads in Muchatha, Kiambaa Constituency.
The KSh.560 million project forms part of the government’s KSh.60 billion investment in constructing 411 kilometres of roads across Kiambu County.
Ruto disclosed that the Mau Mau roads project was between 80 and 90 per cent complete, with the remaining works expected to be finalised by April 2027.
He also announced that the government would begin dualling the Muthaiga-Kiambu Road early next year to ease traffic congestion.
At Matathia in Lari Constituency, the President inspected ongoing works on the 105-kilometre Mau Mau Roads Project, which has a budget of KSh.4.5 billion and is 88 per cent complete.
On healthcare, Ruto revealed that 1.6 million Kiambu residents, representing 65 per cent of the county’s population, had registered under the Social Health Authority (SHA).
He added that the government had released KSh.12.5 billion to cater for medical bills in hospitals across the county.

The President further highlighted investments in 32 modern markets, 17,000 affordable housing units and student hostels targeting 15,000 university, technical college and Kenya Medical Training College students.
He described the investments as unprecedented in the county.

Deputy President Kithure Kindiki, who accompanied Ruto, said previous administrations had not distributed development projects equitably, singling out Lari Constituency as one of the areas that had been neglected.
“President Ruto has ensured that when Kiambu County develops, every part of the county also develops, including Lari,” Kindiki said.
ICT Cabinet Secretary William Kabogo also dismissed claims that political leaders could determine how Kiambu residents vote, maintaining that voters make independent political choices.

items.title: Gachagua vs IEBC: The eligibility battle shaping Kenya 2027
items.description: Former Deputy President Rigathi Gachagua is challenging the IEBC over his 2027 presidential eligibility following his impeachment and a pending court appeal.
content: Former Deputy President Rigathi Gachagua has turned his contested presidential eligibility into a political weapon — and the IEBC’s nervous response suggests the question will define Kenya’s most consequential electoral season in a decade.

Former Deputy President Rigathi Gachagua has publicly challenged the Independent Electoral and Boundaries Commission over its handling of his eligibility to contest the 2027 presidential election, escalating a constitutional dispute that has become one of the defining fault lines of Kenya’s political season and that shows no sign of resolution before the August 2027 General Election.

The confrontation crystallised on 25 November 2026, when the IEBC issued a clarifying statement distancing itself from media reports alleging it had cleared Gachagua to contest, stressing that it had neither approved his candidacy nor made any official determination regarding his legal eligibility. “The Commission wishes to clarify that it has made no such determination,” IEBC chairman Erastus Ethekon said, adding that any formal assessment of Gachagua’s eligibility would only be undertaken at the legally designated stage of the electoral calendar.

Gachagua, characteristically, was not prepared to accept that framing quietly. The Democracy for the Citizens Party leader has consistently maintained that his impeachment from the deputy presidency in October 2024 does not bar him from seeking the country’s highest office. “Am I interested? Why not? I am a candidate to be president of the Republic of Kenya. I am qualified. I have support. I am looking for more support, and I’ll be on the ballot as a candidate for president,” he has said.

The legal argument underpinning his position is not without substance, and it has attracted senior legal endorsement. Senior Counsel Charles Kanjama, President of the Law Society of Kenya, has argued that Gachagua remains eligible to contest for public office because the appellate process has not been exhausted, pointing to Articles 73, 75 and 99 of the Constitution. The High Court upheld Gachagua’s impeachment in June 2026, but his legal team filed an appeal, and that pending appeal is central to the eligibility argument his supporters are advancing.

People’s Liberation Party leader Martha Karua has also defended Gachagua’s eligibility, arguing that the law allows an individual to remain eligible for office until all appeals have been determined. “So long as he has given a notice of appeal, you can’t take away eligibility,” Karua said, drawing a pointed historical comparison: “How did Ruto and Uhuru run for president when they were facing Hague charges?”

The parallel is deliberate and politically loaded. President William Ruto and former President Uhuru Kenyatta both contested and won elections while facing charges at the International Criminal Court — a precedent that Gachagua and his allies cite as evidence that Kenya’s constitutional framework does not extinguish electoral rights simply because legal proceedings are ongoing. Gachagua has made the same comparison himself. “Uhuru Kenyatta and Ruto ran for office while they had cases at The Hague. Kenya’s Constitution is clear that if you have a pending court case, your right to contest for a seat cannot be taken away. So if I want to run, I will run,” he said.

The counter-argument is equally grounded in law. Ferdinand Waititu’s attempt to run for governor in 2022 was thwarted by the IEBC after a High Court ruling confirmed his ineligibility due to impeachment — a precedent that those opposing Gachagua’s candidacy regard as the more directly applicable comparison. The distinction between the ICC cases, which involved criminal charges, and impeachment, which carries a specific constitutional disqualification provision, is one that Kenya’s courts will ultimately have to resolve.

That resolution may not come before the electoral calendar demands a definitive answer. The IEBC has confirmed that registration of candidates for the 2027 General Election has not yet commenced and that eligibility decisions will be made at the appropriate stage of the process in accordance with the law. The commission’s studied neutrality is constitutionally defensible, but politically, it leaves a vacuum that both sides are filling aggressively.

Gachagua’s frustration with the IEBC, however, extends well beyond the eligibility question. He has accused the commission of harbouring a plot to rig the 2027 election using technology from a South Korean company, claiming the firm bungled elections in the Democratic Republic of Congo, the Philippines and Iraq. “IEBC should tell Kenyans what the role of Mining Cabinet Secretary Hassan Joho and IEBC Vice Chairperson Fahima Arafat is in this tendering system,” Gachagua said, alleging the tender was designed to favour a particular company. The IEBC has not publicly addressed those specific allegations.

Gachagua commands a significant voting bloc in Mount Kenya and is believed to have access to a sizeable campaign war chest. His political potency is not seriously disputed, even by his opponents. What is disputed — and what will shape the nature of the opposition coalition heading into 2027 — is whether he will be on the ballot at all, or whether he will exercise his considerable influence as a kingmaker rather than a candidate.

He has emphasised that the opposition must present a single candidate to challenge President Ruto in 2027, highlighting the need to address corruption and end extrajudicial killings, while expressing confidence that the 2027 election would be free and fair despite his concerns about the IEBC’s composition. The tension in that position is obvious: a man who insists he will be a presidential candidate while simultaneously calling for a unified opposition ticket is either building leverage for a negotiated withdrawal or genuinely pursuing both objectives simultaneously.

The IEBC sits uncomfortably at the intersection of these competing pressures. It has walked out on opposition parties during consultative meetings, been accused of institutional bias by Gachagua’s coalition and been defended by the ruling Kenya Kwanza camp as a legitimate and independent body doing its job. Its credibility with the opposition is already fractured — and the eligibility dispute, whatever its legal resolution, is widening that fracture.

For Kenya’s democratic architecture, the stakes of getting this right are significant. A situation in which a major presidential aspirant is excluded from the ballot by the IEBC before his appeals have been heard by the Court of Appeal would provoke a constitutional crisis that the country can ill afford in the months before a general election. A situation in which someone constitutionally ineligible nevertheless appears on the ballot would be equally damaging to institutional credibility.

The courts will decide the eligibility question. The IEBC will implement whatever they decide. But the political temperature generated by the dispute — the accusations, the walkouts, the threats of demonstrations — will shape the character of Kenya’s 2027 campaign long before a single vote is cast.
Gachagua has turned a legal question into a political battleground. In Kenya, that has always been how elections are truly won and lost.

Transport CS Chirchir Announces Tougher Vehicle Inspection, Enforcement on Kenyan Roads
items.description: Kenya plans automated vehicle inspections and digital enforcement under a KSh 30bn action plan targeting a 30% fall in road deaths over five years in Kenya.
content: PAY ATTENTION: TUKO is in WhatsApp Channels now! Subscribe and read news in your favourite messenger.

Transport Cabinet Secretary Davis Chirchir has outlined plans to overhaul motor vehicle inspections in Kenya, introducing automated testing facilities and digital systems as part of a broader push to make roads safer across the country.
Chirchir made the announcement on Thursday, 26 November, at the Africa Road Safety Conference, which was convened by KCB Group and the Global Road Safety Partnership.

The CS said the government aimed to cut road fatalities by more than 30% over the next five years, with a longer-term goal of reducing deaths and injuries by at least 50% by 2030. He reaffirmed the Ministry of Roads and Transport's commitment to achieving those targets through a range of interventions.

He added that enforcement on the roads would be intensified, with authorities cracking down on speeding, drunk driving, dangerous overtaking, overloading and reckless driving. Technology will play a central role in that effort.
Chirchir also announced the establishment of the Kenya Road Assessment Programme (KenRAP), designed to identify high-risk sections of road and prioritise remedial work at accident blackspots.

On public transport, he said operator accountability was being strengthened alongside professional driver training. More than 4,000 public transport personnel and drivers completed training in the past three months, according to the CS.
All these measures fall under the KSh 30 billion Road Safety Action Plan covering 2024 to 2028, which also addresses motorcycle safety and improved enforcement capacity.
ENA Coach issues reminder notice to mums travelling with minors

The announcement arrives against a contentious backdrop. Earlier this year, the National Transport and Safety Authority (NTSA) had proposed rules requiring private vehicles older than four years to undergo annual inspections covering brakes, tyres, steering systems and other safety-critical components.

In July, however, the Senate annulled those rules, raising concerns that the implementation window was too short and that existing inspection facilities were insufficient to handle the volume of private vehicles. Senators also warned that the shortage of inspection centres could leave motorists vulnerable to harassment by enforcement officers.

Chirchir's latest statements suggest the government is pressing ahead with its road safety agenda despite that legislative setback, with a greater emphasis on automated infrastructure to address the capacity concerns that derailed the earlier proposals.

items.title: Kenya Airways Issues Early Warning as Fuel Costs Surge, Earnings Decline
items.description: Kenya Airways warns 2026 earnings could fall at least 25% as fuel costs reach half of operating expenses, following a KSh 17.2bn loss in 2025 amid fuel surge.
content: Search option is now available at TUKO! Feel free to search the content on topics/people you enjoy reading about in the top right corner ;)

Kenya Airways has issued a formal profit warning to investors, disclosing that its earnings for the financial year ending 31 December 2026 are expected to drop by at least 25% compared to 2025 figures.

The announcement, signed by Board Chairman Kiprono Kittony on 26 November 2026, cited soaring fuel costs linked to the ongoing Middle East conflict and widespread supply chain disruptions as the primary drivers of the anticipated decline.
The warning was issued in line with Kenya's Capital Markets (Securities) (Public Offers, Listing and Disclosures) Regulations, 2023.
The Board acknowledged that passenger demand across the aviation sector remains robust, but said external pressures have continued to weigh heavily on the airline's performance.

Fuel costs at Kenya Airways jumped 72% in the first half of 2026, with acting CEO George Kamal stating that fuel now represents up to 50% of total operating costs.

The International Air Transport Association projects jet fuel will average USD 152 (approximately KSh 19,600) per barrel in 2026, nearly 70% above the 2025 average of USD 90 (approximately KSh 11,600).
African carriers face an additional burden, paying around 17% more than the global average owing to limited local refining capacity, transport costs, and taxation.
The Middle East conflict has also forced airlines to reroute flights around affected airspace, stretching journey times and burning more fuel on connections between Africa, Europe, and Asia.

Kenya Airways did attract additional passengers redirected away from Gulf transit hubs, with load factors reaching as high as 99% on select routes, but the sharp rise in operating costs offset much of that revenue gain.
Trump announces fresh tariffs on 14 countries after Supreme Court ruling

The 2026 warning builds on a troubled recent history. In 2025, the airline posted a net loss of KSh 17.2 billion, reversing a net profit of KSh 5.4 billion recorded in 2024, which had been the carrier's first annual profit in over a decade.
Total income fell to KSh 161.5 billion in 2025, down from KSh 188.5 billion the previous year.

Much of that decline stemmed from the temporary grounding of three Boeing 787-8 Dreamliner aircraft due to supply chain difficulties, which cut capacity by 18% and reduced passenger numbers by roughly 13%.

The first half of 2026 showed no meaningful recovery. Although revenue grew 9% to KSh 81 billion, the airline still posted a loss after tax of KSh 16.1 billion, compared to KSh 12.2 billion over the same period in 2025.

Finance costs climbed 11.1% to KSh 12.4 billion, the basic loss per share reached KSh 2.94, and negative equity widened to KSh 132.1 billion from KSh 118.3 billion, with total liabilities rising 6% to KSh 315.3 billion.

Looking ahead to 2027, the airline said it would prioritise restoring its full fleet, reducing costs, conserving cash, and completing a capital-raising exercise designed to stabilise its balance sheet and support long-term growth.

items.title: Absa Bank Kenya Reports Kshs. 15.3 Billion Profit After Tax for Nine Months to September 2026
items.description: Absa Bank Kenya PLC recorded a return on equity of 19.9%, reflecting continued business resilience and the execution of its customer-focused growth strategy
content: Absa Bank Kenya PLC has reported a profit after tax of Kshs. 15.3 billion for the nine months ended September 30, 2026, supported by growth in customer lending, deposits and total assets, alongside strong capital and liquidity positions.
Absa Bank Kenya PLC recorded a return on equity of 19.9%, reflecting continued business resilience and the execution of its customer-focused growth strategy amid a lower interest rate environment.
According to its nine-month financial performance, customer assets grew by 11% to Kshs. 342.5 billion, while customer deposits increased by 6% to Kshs. 408 billion.

Total assets rose by 9% to Kshs. 604.1 billion, crossing the Kshs. 600 billion milestone for the first time and strengthening the bank’s capacity to finance businesses, households and key sectors of the Kenyan economy.
The growth in customer financing reflects increased support for individuals, entrepreneurs and businesses seeking capital to invest, expand operations and achieve their financial ambitions.
Customer deposits also increased, highlighting continued confidence in Absa Bank Kenya as a financial partner and the growing relevance of its banking solutions.
The bank said its balance sheet expansion was driven by deeper customer relationships and increased access to financial services.
Absa Bank Kenya posts Sh10.5 billion half-year profit
Absa Bank Kenya generated total revenue of Kshs. 44.7 billion during the nine-month period, supported by balance sheet growth and disciplined management of funding costs.
Net interest income stood at Kshs. 32.3 billion, recording growth in each successive quarter, while non-interest income contributed Kshs. 12.4 billion.
The bank said its third quarter delivered its strongest revenue performance of 2026, reflecting sustained business momentum despite the lower interest rate environment.

Commenting on the results, Absa Bank Kenya Managing Director and Chief Executive Officer Yusuf Omari said the performance demonstrated customer confidence and the strength of relationships built across the bank’s franchise.

“Our nine-month performance reflects the trust that customers continue to place in Absa and the strength of the relationships we have built across our franchise. In a lower interest rate environment, we remained focused on supporting our customers’ ambitions through accessible financing, innovative solutions and seamless banking experiences,” said Omari.
He added that the customer-led approach supported growth in both lending and deposits, with momentum building throughout the year.
The bank continued to strengthen its portfolio quality while maintaining disciplined cost management and investing in technology, talent and business transformation.
Its cost-to-income ratio closed at 42%, remaining within the bank’s strategic plan.
Asset quality also improved, with the non-performing loans (NPL) ratio declining to 9.8%, which the bank said remained below industry levels.
The loan loss ratio improved to 2.0%, reflecting better portfolio performance and effective risk management.
Absa Bank Kenya’s capital adequacy ratio stood at 19.3%, while liquidity reserves were maintained at 44.7%, providing a strong financial position to support future lending and business growth.
The bank’s return on equity of 19.9% also demonstrated its continued ability to generate value for shareholders.
Absa commits Shs230M to new global multi-asset investment fund
Digital transformation remained a key pillar of Absa Bank Kenya’s growth strategy during the reporting period.
One of the notable developments was the launch of Absa Next , described by the bank as Kenya’s first integrated digital financial ecosystem.
The platform brings together banking, savings, investments, credit and lifestyle services in one digital environment accessible to both Absa customers and non-customers.
The initiative is designed to simplify access to financial services while providing customers with a more integrated experience beyond traditional banking.

Absa also expanded its affluent banking proposition through the introduction of Kenya’s first co-branded travel and lifestyle credit card, extending customer benefits into travel and lifestyle services.
Absa Asset Management Limited strengthened its investment offering through the launch of two new Global Multi-Asset Special Funds.
The funds are denominated in Kenya shillings and US dollars, providing investors with additional investment options and opportunities to diversify their portfolios.
The launches form part of the wider group’s strategy to deepen customer engagement, strengthen its investment management business and diversify revenue streams.
Co-op Bank Q3 net profit hits Sh27.4bn; interim dividend rises 50pc
Strategic partnerships continued to play an important role in expanding Absa’s financial and non-financial solutions.
The bank said its collaborations enabled it to provide tailored solutions that respond to the changing needs of customers while supporting business development and economic inclusion.
In Kenya, Absa facilitated financing for solar-powered cold storage solutions aimed at addressing gaps in the agricultural value chain and reducing post-harvest losses.
The initiative seeks to strengthen agricultural productivity by improving storage infrastructure and helping farmers and other value-chain players preserve their produce.

The bank also supported the third edition of a hackathon in Kenya through an established partnership, providing a platform for young women to develop technology-driven solutions to practical challenges.
These initiatives demonstrate the bank’s continued focus on using financial services and strategic partnerships to promote innovation, sustainability and inclusive economic growth.
Absa Bank Kenya said it would continue investing in digital platforms, strategic partnerships and customer relationships as it pursues its ambition of becoming the financial partner of choice.

The bank’s strategy is anchored on its purpose of Empowering Africa’s tomorrow, together… one story at a time , with a focus on delivering customer-led innovation and sustainable value for customers, communities and shareholders.

“As we execute the next phase of our strategy, our ambition remains clear on being the financial partner of choice by delivering customer-led innovation, market-leading solutions and sustainable growth across all our businesses,” said Omari.
He noted that the bank’s strong capital position, expanding digital ecosystem and diversified franchise provided a solid foundation for capturing emerging opportunities and creating long-term value.

Absa Bank Kenya’s nine-month results highlight the resilience of its banking operations, supported by balance sheet expansion, improving asset quality, digital innovation and continued investment in Kenya’s economic development.

The National Police Service has gazetted 10 extra recruitment centres for its Police Constable intake exercise, after the venues were accidentally left out of the original advertisement published on 20 November 2026.
The addendum, signed by Inspector General Douglas Kanja Kirocho, raises the total number of recruitment centres nationwide to 433, up from the 423 initially announced .
The recruitment exercise remains scheduled for Thursday, 10 December 2026, running from 8:00 a.m. to 5:00 p.m. across the country.
The 10 newly added centres are spread across six counties, with Marsabit accounting for four of them: Uran, Korr, Sagante, and Illeret.

The additions are concentrated in the northern and western parts of the country, reducing the distance candidates in those sub-counties would otherwise need to travel.
All other details from the original advertisement, including eligibility requirements and the application process, remain unchanged.

As reported earlier, the recruitment exercise is free and open to all eligible Kenyan citizens. Candidates must be aged between 18 and 28 years, hold a valid national identity card, and have attained a minimum KCSE mean grade of D+, with at least a D+ in English or Kiswahili.

Female applicants must not be pregnant at the time of recruitment or during training.
On the day of the exercise, candidates are required to present originals and copies of their academic certificates, their Kenya National Identity Card, and a birth certificate.
Those reporting to the NYS Headquarters in Ruaraka must additionally bring an NYS discharge certificate showing a conduct rating of at least "Good."
The National Police Service reiterated that attempting to bribe officials or submitting false information during the recruitment process constitutes a criminal offence.

Members of the public who suspect any malpractice are encouraged to report it at the nearest police station or through the toll-free lines 999, 911, 112, or via the DCI hotline 0800 722 203. The service has committed to treating all such reports in strict confidence.

Former Governor jailed 25 years for killing pregnant girlfriend
items.description: Zacharia Okoth Obado sentenced to 25 years for murdering university student Sharon Otieno after eight-year legal battle.
content: Obado, however, has filed a notice of appeal challenging both his conviction and the 25-year sentence. His lawyer, Senior Counsel Kioko Kilukumi, submitted the notice on Friday, indicating that the former governor intends to contest the High Court’s July 23 decision before the Court of Appeal.

Former Migori County Governor Zacharia Okoth Obado has been sentenced to 25 years in prison for the 2018 murder of university student Sharon Belyne Otieno, bringing a dramatic turn to an eight-year legal battle that has drawn widespread attention in Kenya.
Obado was sentenced on Friday, November 27, 2026, by High Court Judge Cecilia Wairimu Githua at the Milimani Law Courts in Nairobi, Kenya after being found guilty of murder in July.
His former personal assistant, Michael Juma Oyamo, also received a 25-year prison sentence, while former Migori County Clerk Caspal Ajwang Obiero was sentenced to 18 years.

In her sentencing remarks, Justice Githua described Obado as the principal architect of the criminal enterprise that led to Sharon’s death, saying he supplied the motive and financial resources used to facilitate the killing.
The judge found that the three accused acted jointly with others who were not before the court, with each playing a distinct role in the plan that resulted in the murder.

Obado, however, has filed a notice of appeal challenging both his conviction and the 25-year sentence. His lawyer, Senior Counsel Kioko Kilukumi, submitted the notice on Friday, indicating that the former governor intends to contest the High Court’s July 23 decision before the Court of Appeal.
The appeal means the case, which began in 2018, is set to enter another legal phase.
Obado’s journey to political prominence began far from the corridors of county power.

Born in 1957, he trained as an educationist and worked as a teacher before venturing into business, particularly sugarcane farming. His professional background included teaching at Rapogi High School and Taranganya Boys High School.
He later became involved in the sugar industry and served as chairman of the Kenya Sugar Board, a position that helped establish his influence among farmers and business stakeholders in the region.
His entry into politics followed an unsuccessful attempt to win the Uriri parliamentary seat in 2007.

Obado subsequently shifted his ambition to the governorship of Migori County ahead of Kenya’s 2013 General Election. After falling out with the Orange Democratic Movement (ODM) during the party’s nomination process, he contested under the People’s Democratic Party (PDP).
He defeated ODM candidate Edward Oyugi to become Migori’s first governor following the introduction of devolved government.
In 2017, Obado returned to ODM, secured its nomination and won re-election, defeating former Cabinet minister Ochilo Ayacko.
His two terms in office placed him among the influential political figures in western Kenya. But his political career was later overshadowed by the murder investigation involving Sharon Otieno.
Sharon, a 26-year-old Rongo University student, was seven months pregnant when she was killed in September 2018.
The High Court established that she was in an intimate relationship with Obado and that he was the biological father of her unborn child.

The case attracted national attention after Sharon’s disappearance and subsequent discovery of her body. The prosecution alleged that her murder was connected to the relationship and the circumstances surrounding her pregnancy.
Evidence presented during the trial included testimony from 42 witnesses and 81 exhibits.
Obado, Oyamo and Obiero denied the murder charges when they were arraigned in October 2018.
The proceedings continued for years, with the trial affected by legal applications, procedural delays and the COVID-19 pandemic.
On July 23, 2026, Justice Githua convicted the three men, finding that they had acted together in a common criminal plan that led to Sharon’s death.
The court subsequently considered their individual roles, the aggravating circumstances of the offence and the mitigation presented before imposing the sentences on November 27.

In explaining the sentence, Justice Githua said Obado’s role was central to the murder plot. She found that he provided the motive, instigated the killing and supplied financial resources to facilitate its execution.
Oyamo, the former personal assistant, was found to have played a role in operationalising and facilitating the plan, while Obiero provided logistical assistance.
The court held that the aggravating circumstances outweighed the mitigating factors presented by the convicts.

Sharon’s family had asked the court to consider a non-custodial sentence for Obado, citing his financial support for her children. The judge rejected that request, warning that financial assistance to a victim’s family should not become a means of avoiding imprisonment for a serious crime.
The court also declined to award compensation to the family, saying there was insufficient evidence to determine the extent of the loss and damage for that purpose.

Obado’s notice of appeal was filed shortly after the sentencing. His lawyer also requested certified copies of the proceedings, judgment and sentencing decision to facilitate the preparation of the appeal.
The former governor is challenging both the July conviction and the prison term imposed on him.

Sharon’s family has also expressed dissatisfaction with the sentences and indicated its intention to challenge the punishment, arguing that the outcome did not fully address its expectations of justice.

The Kenya Meteorological Service Authority has forecast largely dry weather across most parts of the country, with only a few counties expected to receive light rainfall and isolated thunderstorms on Saturday, November 28.

In its daily weather forecast issued on Friday, November 27, the department indicated that most counties would experience partly cloudy conditions at night, followed by sunny intervals in the morning and afternoon.
The outlook could concern farmers in areas relying on seasonal rainfall for crop production, particularly those whose agricultural activities depend on consistent precipitation.
However, the department did not issue a prolonged dry spell or drought warning, but indicated that rainfall would remain limited to a few locations.

In the Eastern region, Marsabit, Meru, Tharaka-Nithi, Embu, Kitui, Machakos and Makueni are expected to receive varying amounts of light rainfall, with some areas likely to experience thunderstorms in the afternoon.
Murang'a and Kiambu are also expected to receive light showers and thunderstorms in a few places during the afternoon.
Kakamega is forecast to experience isolated showers and thunderstorms at night, although sunny intervals are expected during the day.
The rest of the counties, including Nairobi, Uasin Gishu, Nakuru, Kisumu , Busia, Siaya, Kericho, Bomet and Trans Nzoia, are expected to experience mainly sunny intervals.

Besides the rainfall outlook, the department warned of strong southerly to southeasterly winds exceeding 25 knots (12.5 metres per second) in parts of Marsabit and Turkana counties.
Residents in the affected areas should take precautions against the potentially disruptive winds.

The forecast also showed significant temperature variations across the country. Mandera is expected to record one of the highest maximum temperatures at 36°C, alongside Tana River and Turkana, which will experience similarly hot conditions.
On the other hand, Nyandarua is expected to record a minimum temperature of 11°C, making it one of the coldest counties during the forecast period.
Uasin Gishu, Narok and Kericho are expected to record minimum temperatures of 12°C. The forecast is valid from 9pm on Friday, November 27, to 9pm on Saturday, November 28.

items.title: Marc Marquez retires after eighth MotoGP title in Valencia
items.description: Marc Marquez announced his retirement from MotoGP at Valencia after winning his eighth world championship in 2026, equalling Giacomo Agostini's all-time record.
content: The greatest motorcycle racer of his generation closes a career defined by genius, injury, comeback and history — leaving MotoGP without its most compelling protagonist.

Marc Marquez announced his retirement from MotoGP on Friday at the Circuit Ricardo Tormo in Valencia, ending one of the most extraordinary careers in motorsport history after the Spaniard secured a record-equalling eighth premier-class world championship in Portugal with a round to spare.

The announcement stunned a paddock that had expected Marquez to lead the sport into its new 850cc era. He had signed a contract extension with Ducati earlier in 2026, due to run until 2028. What followed was a shoulder surgery — his fourth significant operation — a fractured foot, an absence from his home Grand Prix and a 102-point deficit in the championship standings. That he responded by winning six of the next nine rounds and retaining the title makes the retirement’s timing all the more remarkable. He leaves not in decline but at the precise moment of his greatest triumph.

“Thank you to everyone who’s been part of the journey,” he said in a video recorded in the Valencia garage. “I hope you’ve enjoyed it as much as I have. This will be my last race in MotoGP. We made history.”

They did. Eight world championships. A debut title in 2013 at 20 years old, making him the youngest premier-class champion the sport had seen. Six further crowns with Honda before injury, serial surgery and mechanical decline stripped him of everything except the stubbornness to continue. A move to Gresini Racing on year-old Ducati machinery. A resurrection. Then the factory Ducati seat, a seventh title in Japan in 2025 — 2,184 days after his sixth — and now an eighth that required him to overturn a deficit that would have ended most riders’ seasons entirely.

Marquez said he made the decision to retire during the Japanese Grand Prix, before the season’s conclusion, as the cumulative physical and mental cost of repeated injuries began to outweigh his appetite for competition. “Sometimes you need to understand the situation, but it’s true that the situation this year was on the limit,” he said. Brief recurrences of double vision at the Indonesian and French Grands Prix — the neurological legacy of a catastrophic 2011 crash — made him more conservative in the season’s second half. “It was one of the main reasons why I controlled the risk and why I crashed less,” he acknowledged.

The announcement brought tears to the Ducati garage and to the grandstands at Valencia. Jorge Martin, his principal title rival, looked stunned. Alex Marquez, told of the decision weeks earlier in Japan, watched with the quiet gravity of a man who had spent a career observing his brother from an impossible distance.

The arc of Marquez’s story is unlike any other in the sport’s modern era. He arrived in 2013 and immediately won, as though the premier class were simply the next natural step. By 2019, six championships in and apparently unbeatable, prolonged dominance seemed inevitable. Then Jerez in 2020: a crash, a broken arm, a botched recovery, three more surgeries and years spent riding compromised equipment into circuits he had once dismantled with total authority.

He considered stopping. He admitted as much. That he chose instead to change manufacturer, rebuild on slower machinery and reconstruct his belief from the ground up is the detail that separates his story from the standard narrative of sporting greatness. When he finally won again — ending a 1,043-day drought in Aragon — it carried the weight of everything that had come before it.

The symbolic moment came in Portugal, where Giacomo Agostini presented him with a commemorative golden helmet as a graphic of a goat — shorthand for the greatest of all time — appeared on the screen behind him. Marquez, characteristically, resisted the superlative. “I do not agree that I’m the greatest rider. I don’t like it. I’m one of the greatest, yes, because the numbers are there,” he said.
The numbers, and the story behind them, suggest the distinction is academic.

Valencia’s final lap will represent the last time the most gifted, most maddening and most compelling motorcycle racer of his generation lines up on a MotoGP grid. After everything — the titles, the surgeries, the comebacks — Marc Marquez is going out entirely on his own terms.

items.title: Kicosca Games Promote National Unity
items.description: Kicosca Games Promote National Unity Kenya News Agency
content: The 13th Edition of the Kenya Inter-Counties Sports and Cultural Association (KICOSCA) Games has continued to demonstrate the power of sports and cultural exchange in bringing Kenyans together, with public servants from across the 47 counties using the national event to strengthen friendships, celebrate diversity and promote national cohesion.

Hosted by West Pokot County, the week-long sporting extravaganza has brought together thousands of participants, officials and spectators in an atmosphere of friendly competition, cultural interaction and national unity.

Beyond the pursuit of trophies and medals, the games have provided a platform for workers from different counties, communities and cultural backgrounds to interact, appreciate one another and reinforce the shared identity of being Kenyan.

Bungoma Governor Kenneth Lusaka, who was the guest of the day’s activities, said KICOSCA had remained an important national platform for promoting unity since its establishment following the introduction of devolution.

Lusaka noted that although counties have different languages, traditions and cultural identities, sporting activities provide an opportunity for Kenyans to interact beyond their geographical and cultural differences.
He said the primary objective of the games should not be winning trophies but building lasting relationships and strengthening the bonds that hold the country together.

“The main aim is not necessarily to win, but to bond. These games bring people together from different counties, speaking different languages and practising different cultures. It is one way of fighting tribalism and promoting national cohesion,” said Lusaka.

He encouraged participants to use the opportunity to establish friendships and appreciate the country’s diversity, adding that they should return to their respective counties having made new friends and developed a stronger sense of national belonging.
“When you leave here, you should have made friends from other counties and understood that despite our differences, Kenya is one,” he added.
His sentiments were echoed by West Pokot Governor Simon Kachapin, who is hosting the 13th edition in his capacity as the patron of the whole event.

Kachapin expressed excitement over his county’s performance across the various sporting disciplines, saying the home teams had demonstrated determination and competitive spirit as they sought to defend the county’s sporting reputation.
He noted that hosting the national games was an opportunity for West Pokot to showcase its hospitality, cultural heritage and potential while creating economic opportunities for local residents.
The Governor said the influx of participants and visitors had stimulated business activities, particularly in hospitality, accommodation, transport, food vending and other small-scale enterprises.
He observed that such national events provide counties with an opportunity to open up their economies, attract visitors and promote destinations that may otherwise receive limited national attention.

Kachapin said the benefits of the tournament extended beyond the sporting arenas, as interactions among participants were helping strengthen relationships between county governments and communities across the country.

The Governor today hosted his Bungoma counterpart, Lusaka, at his official residence before the two leaders joined spectators at Talau and Kapenguria Boys Senior School to follow the football and volleyball encounters.
The visit highlighted the spirit of friendship and cooperation that the tournament seeks to promote among county governments and their leadership.
Meanwhile, competition has intensified as teams enter the decisive knockout stages, with hosts West Pokot among the counties making impressive progress.

Football attracted considerable attention on Day Four after West Pokot defeated Kilifi 3-0 at Makutano Stadium to secure a place in the men’s quarter-finals. Bungoma also progressed after edging Machakos 5-4 in a penalty shootout following a tightly contested encounter.
The men’s football quarter-final fixtures scheduled for Friday will see West Pokot face Bungoma, Kisumu take on Siaya, Kakamega meet Nyandarua, while Nairobi will battle Embu at different venues.

In women’s volleyball, West Pokot maintained its impressive run with a 3-1 victory over Nyandarua at Kapenguria Boys Senior School. The hosts won the opening two sets 25-18 and 25-18 before Nyandarua recovered to take the third set 28-26. West Pokot, however, regained control to win the fourth set 25-20 and advance to the quarter-finals.
Other teams that secured places in the last eight included Kakamega, Murang’a, Uasin Gishu, Bungoma and Nandi, following victories over their respective opponents.

Basketball has also provided entertaining encounters, with Nairobi narrowly defeating Kakamega 68-67 in the men’s category, while Kiambu registered a 70-26 victory over Uasin Gishu. Turkana also impressed with a 78-38 win against Narok.

In the women’s category, Vihiga defeated Kiambu 34-28, while Turkana overcame Meru 43-19. The women’s basketball quarter-finals will feature Kisumu against Narok, Nairobi against Machakos, Kisii against Turkana and Uasin Gishu against Vihiga.

Away from the competitive arenas, the cultural activities have offered counties an opportunity to showcase their distinct identities through traditional dances, music and other cultural presentations. These displays have provided an important reminder that the country’s diversity remains a source of strength and shared heritage.

The organisation of the games has also received positive feedback, with activities proceeding smoothly and scheduled competitions taking place without reported security incidents or major disruptions.

The venues have been adequately distributed across the host area, with participants able to access the different sporting facilities despite some distances between competition centres. The arrangements have enabled teams to participate in their respective disciplines while spectators move between venues to support their counties.
As the tournament progresses towards its conclusion, West Pokot is enjoying the opportunity to host the country and demonstrate its capacity to organise national events.

Ultimately, the significance of KICOSCA extends beyond the medals and championship titles. By bringing together public servants from all corners of Kenya, the games reinforce the spirit of devolution, encourage inter-county cooperation and promote a national identity that transcends ethnic and geographical boundaries.

For West Pokot, the event is not only a sporting milestone but also an opportunity to demonstrate that sports, culture and hospitality can serve as powerful instruments for economic development and national unity.

items.title: Kenya, Zimbabwe strengthen bilateral ties through media cooperation
items.description: Kenya, Zimbabwe strengthen bilateral ties through media cooperation Kenya News Agency
content: Kenya and Zimbabwe have formalised cooperation in the media and information sector following the signing of a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) between Kenya News Agency (KNA) and Zimbabwe’s Inter-African News Agency (NEW ZIANA).

The MoU was signed at State House, Nairobi, by Kenya’s Principal Secretary for Broadcasting and Telecommunications, Stephen Isaboke, and Zimbabwe’s Permanent Secretary for Information, Publicity and Broadcasting Services, Nick Ndabaningi Mangwana.
The signing follows Zimbabwean President Dr Emmerson Dambudzo Mnangagwa’s state visit to Kenya, where he held bilateral talks with President William Ruto at State House.

Speaking during the engagement, PS Isaboke said the MoU seeks to strengthen media cooperation between the two countries through enhanced collaboration, information sharing and professional engagement.

“As part of this engagement, I signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) between the Kenya News Agency (KNA) and the Zimbabwe Inter-African News Agency (NEW ZIANA), alongside my Zimbabwean counterpart, the Permanent Secretary for Information, Publicity and Broadcasting Services, Mr Nick Ndavaningi Mangwana,” the PS said.
He revealed that the signing formed part of the broader bilateral engagements aimed at deepening cooperation and formalising agreements of mutual interest between the two countries.
“Today, I participated in the Kenya–Zimbabwe bilateral meeting held during the State Visit of President Emmerson Dambudzo Mnangagwa of Zimbabwe, hosted by President Dr William Ruto,” he said.

PS Isaboke said the MoU will provide a framework for the exchange of news and multimedia content, professional capacity building, sharing of knowledge and technical expertise, as well as collaboration in journalism and Information and Communication Technology (ICT).

“The MoU will provide a framework for the exchange of news and multimedia content, professional capacity building, sharing of knowledge and technical expertise, as well as collaboration in journalism and Information and Communication Technology (ICT),” he explained.

The MoU will pave the way for a stronger partnership between the two national news agencies, further enhancing institutional collaboration, promoting information sharing and facilitating the exchange of professional knowledge and expertise.
Isaboke added that the MoU will also promote people-to-people relations and enhance the visibility of African perspectives on regional and international media platforms.

The PS also underscored the importance of intra-African media cooperation in empowering African countries to tell their own stories, shape their narratives and showcase the continent’s development, innovation, cultural diversity and economic opportunities.

Isaboke revealed that the partnership will provide the Kenya News Agency (KNA) with an opportunity to strengthen its regional media presence, expand content exchange with NEW ZIANA and enhance the coverage and sharing of African stories across regional and international media platforms.

The partnership will also enhance information exchange between KNA and NEW ZIANA, promote the sharing of accurate and credible information, and strengthen the dissemination of African stories across regional and international media platforms.

“This partnership is an important step towards strengthening media cooperation, enhancing the flow of credible information and deepening the longstanding friendship between Kenya and Zimbabwe,” he said.
Established in 1963, the Kenya News Agency (KNA) is the government’s flagship news agency under the Directorate of Information, State Department for Broadcasting and Telecommunications.

The Agency plays a vital role in gathering, processing and disseminating credible, accurate and timely news and information to support national development and enable the public to make informed decisions.

With a presence in all 47 counties and 25 sub-county offices, KNA is strategically positioned to leverage the partnership to expand its reach, strengthen its visibility and enhance the sharing of Kenyan stories with regional and international audiences.

The collaboration with NEW ZIANA is expected to complement KNA’s mandate by creating opportunities for enhanced content exchange and professional collaboration and, more so, promote dissemination of credible African perspectives and news on the global media stage.
It will further contribute to the growth of Africa’s information ecosystem and advance the broader aspirations of continental integration.

Kenya Needs Its Own AI Models, Data Centres And Energy, Ndemo Says
items.description: The former ambassador argues that locally trained models, built around African languages and contexts, are essential to protecting data, expanding access and creating jobs.
content: Kenya must build its own artificial intelligence infrastructure and train models in local languages if it is to retain control of its data, develop relevant AI applications and capture more economic value from the technology, Dr Bitange Ndemo has said.

Speaking during a session on Sovereign AI at the CIO100 Symposium & Awards 2026 in Diani, the former Ambassador to Belgium and the European Union argued that relying on foreign AI models exposes African countries to external decisions over access, data and the technologies their economies increasingly depend on.
“Everybody can actually make their own AI which understands the local context,” Ndemo said, arguing that models must be trained to understand local laws, cultures and languages.

He described AI as a child’s brain that needs to be trained and shaped by its environment. A model developed elsewhere, he argued, may not adequately understand the differences between Kenyan, Tanzanian and Ugandan law, or the social and cultural contexts in which people use technology.

For Ndemo, sovereignty goes beyond hosting data locally. It requires countries to develop the supporting infrastructure, including data centres, reliable energy, connectivity, skilled engineers and locally trained language models.
Local languages are central to AI adoption
Ndemo said the limitations of foreign models become particularly significant when AI is expected to address problems rooted in local economic and social realities.

He argued that African languages do not always have direct equivalents for concepts such as data, productivity and predictability. Without the vocabulary to communicate these ideas accurately, he said, AI systems risk reproducing gaps in how development challenges are understood and addressed.
He used poverty as an example, arguing that efforts to address it have often failed to communicate the practical knowledge people need to improve their livelihoods.

In agriculture, he said, farmers need information that helps them use fewer resources to produce more. Locally trained models could help communicate such knowledge in languages and contexts that communities understand.

Ndemo also pointed to education, arguing that learning in a familiar language can improve comprehension. Personalised AI, he said, could adapt how information is delivered to an individual’s pace of understanding, potentially reaching learners who struggle in conventional classroom settings.

He said locally developed models could also help bridge the gap between formal education and practical knowledge, using the example of rural builders who understand roof angles through experience even when they may not connect that knowledge to classroom mathematics.
Sovereignty requires infrastructure and energy
Ndemo warned that dependence on foreign AI providers creates strategic risks for countries that lack control over the models they use.

He raised the possibility of an external provider restricting access to its services following a political or commercial decision, leaving businesses and public institutions without systems on which they have come to rely.
He also questioned the value African countries receive when they provide data that can be used elsewhere to develop commercial products, including medicines.
His argument was that African countries should retain greater control over the data and infrastructure needed to develop their own AI capabilities.

Energy, he said, is a critical part of that ambition. He urged African governments and investors to direct more capital towards electricity generation, arguing that data centres and GPU infrastructure require reliable and affordable power.

Citing Ethiopia’s investments in electricity generation, Ndemo said the country had moved ahead with large-scale energy projects that could support industrial activity and emerging technology industries.
He argued that Kenya should use available land and energy resources to attract infrastructure investment, create employment and support a growing cloud economy.
Building a talent pipeline and local AI industry
Ndemo said sovereign AI would also require sustained investment in engineers and other technical professionals who can build, train and maintain local systems.

He argued that developing local language models could create opportunities for African startups, content creators and technology businesses, while allowing countries to address challenges that imported systems may not adequately understand.

Among the potential applications he cited was healthcare. He described the use of smartphone-based tools to help health workers identify possible tuberculosis cases, illustrating how AI could support earlier diagnosis and intervention.
He also said locally developed systems could help create jobs by enabling businesses to build products and services around models trained for African markets.
Ndemo disclosed that he was working towards developing a Kenyan AI model and was seeking local partners willing to test and support the initiative before wider commercial participation.

He said the intention was to make a basic model available for people to begin using, with a broader national AI service offering that could support developers and businesses. He invited interested organisations to engage with the initiative, including through potential subscriptions to solutions built on the model.

His message to technology leaders was that AI sovereignty should not be reduced to a debate about foreign versus local software. It should be treated as a national capability involving energy, infrastructure, data, skills and language.
“Everything needed already exists. Only the model is missing,” Ndemo said.

items.title: Kenyan Researchers Secure Funding to Study Climate’S Impact on Health
items.description: By Jean-Pierre A.
content: Scientists led by the Kenya Medical Research Institute (KEMRI) have received £2.3 million (about KSh 394 million) to study how heat, drought, malaria, snakebite, hunger and mental distress pile up on the same households in Turkana County. The researchers say these overlapping burdens have gone largely unmeasured.
The three-year study, Strategic Health Integration for Equitable and Localized Decision-making (SHIELD), is funded by the UK-based Wellcome Trust.

“A single family may face heat from outdoor work and a poorly insulated home, food and water shortages, mosquitoes breeding around water points, and snakes in grazing and water-collection areas, all at the same time,” said Dr Daniel Kwaro, the study’s principal investigator.

Dr Kwaro said that, to the best of his knowledge, this is the first project to consider these risks together, because health and weather systems record them separately. Drought is logged without information on who is exposed, and clinics record illness without its link to the climate.
“Heat illness, from fainting to heatstroke, is rarely recorded as heat illness, and even when a clinic sees it, the link to the weather is usually lost,” Dr Kwaro said.
Dr Patrick Amoth, Director General for Health, said the government needs this evidence because the country’s health information systems are built to count diseases one at a time.
“If we, as a government, cannot see that burden, we cannot plan or budget for it, or act before it becomes a crisis,” Dr Amoth said at the launch of the project today in Nairobi.

Over three years, researchers will survey refugee and host households across four seasons, fit 100 adults with smartwatches to measure heat strain, trap mosquitoes monthly, survey snakes in areas where people are bitten, and compare clinic records with what households report. With Turkana County and humanitarian agencies, the team will turn the findings into a climate-health dashboard, a budgeting tool and an early-warning system that can help governments plan.

Dr Gilchrist Lokoel, Turkana County’s Chief Officer of Health, told reporters at the launch that the county was waiting for the evidence, given the sharp changes it has seen in drought, heat and heat-related illness.

Malaria is one of the risks the study will track. Dr Eric Ochomo, head of entomology at KEMRI and a member of the SHIELD team, said a rise of about one degree Celsius had let mosquitoes thrive in places where they were not traditionally found. Anopheles stephensi , a malaria mosquito native to South Asia and the Middle East, was first confirmed in Kenya in 2022 and has since been found in 13 counties, he said. Dr Ochomo said the response would need community awareness as well as science.

“Covering tanks, screening inlets and draining spillage at tap stands and boreholes would stop stored water from breeding mosquitoes, and that work belongs in malaria control, including surveillance for species of mosquitoes, such as the Anopheles stephensi,” Dr Ochomo said.

The researchers describe Turkana as a “sentinel” setting. It does not represent the whole country or continent, but it lets them study how overlapping risks build up, with lessons for similar dryland and refugee-hosting areas.
